intro:
IKEA furniture gets a bad reputation in small apartments, and most of it is unfair. The pieces themselves are simple, affordable and sized for tight rooms. What makes them look flat-pack is leaving them exactly as they come out of the box, sitting a few inches short of the wall with nothing anchoring them to the room.

The hacks below fix that. Each one starts with a well-known IKEA piece and adds one or two simple changes: trim that closes the gap to the ceiling, legs that lift a boxy dresser off the floor, paint that unifies mismatched units, or hardware that makes a basic cabinet feel chosen rather than assembled. Most are renter-friendly, and the few that are not say so clearly.

sections.title: 1. Turn a KALLAX Into a Built-In Window Seat
sections.content:
Place a KALLAX shelf unit on its side beneath a window, add a plywood base to bring it to seat height, and top it with a custom-cut cushion in a durable fabric. The cubes below become shoe, book and blanket storage, and the whole thing reads as a built-in bench rather than a shelf lying on its side.

Finish the edges with a strip of trim painted to match your wall, and add a few throw pillows in the same palette as the room. Anchor the unit to the wall for safety, especially if children will climb on it. In a rental, skip the trim and use a cushion with a non-slip base instead, so the whole seat can move out with you.

sections.title: 2. Give a BILLY Bookcase a Built-In Look With Trim and Paint
sections.content:
A BILLY bookcase looks instantly more expensive when it reaches the ceiling and meets the wall without gaps. Add a simple board across the top to close the space above the unit, run thin trim down the sides where it meets the wall, and paint the whole assembly, trim included, in one color.

Painting the back panel the same color as the shelves is the detail that sells it. Add small brass or matte black knobs to the lower doors if your unit has them, and style the shelves with books grouped by height rather than packed edge to edge. This is a permanent-looking change, so renters should use removable trim attached with adhesive strips instead of nails.

sections.title: 3. Raise a MALM Dresser on Furniture Legs
sections.content:
A MALM dresser sits low and flat on the floor, which is why it can read as a plain box. Screw on four short tapered or turned furniture legs and the same dresser suddenly has the proportions of a mid-century piece, with a shadow gap underneath that makes a small bedroom feel less crowded.

Choose legs around four to six inches tall so the drawers stay easy to reach, and add felt pads to protect the floor. Swap the standard pulls for leather tabs or slim brass bars at the same time for a bigger transformation. This hack needs only a drill and a mounting plate kit, and it is fully reversible, which makes it ideal for renters.

sections.title: 4. Build a Room Divider From Two KALLAX Units
sections.content:
In a studio, two KALLAX units placed back to back create a freestanding divider that separates a sleeping area from a living area without blocking light completely. Fill the cubes facing the living side with books and plants, and use the bedroom side for folded clothes in fabric bins.

Top the units with a single long board to join them into one piece of furniture and give you a display shelf. Keep the total height at four cubes or fewer so the room still feels open, and anchor each unit to the other with brackets. Because nothing is attached to the walls, this divider moves with you when your lease ends.

sections.title: 5. Turn BESTA Units Into a Floating Media Wall
sections.content:
Wall-mounted BESTA cabinets hung in a row beneath a television create the look of a floating media console for a fraction of the cost of a custom unit. Mount them at a consistent height, leave a gap of a few inches to the floor, and run the television cables through a paintable cord channel down to the nearest outlet.

Use a mix of open frames and closed doors so the wall does not become one solid block, and add warm LED strip lighting underneath the cabinets to make the whole wall glow at night. This hack requires drilling into studs and a level, so it suits owners or renters with permission to mount. Always check the weight rating of your wall fixings before loading the cabinets.

sections.title: 6. Hack a PAX Wardrobe Into a Built-In Closet
sections.content:
A PAX wardrobe becomes a built-in closet when you fill the gap above it. Measure from the top of the frame to the ceiling, build a simple filler panel from painted plywood, and add crown-style trim across the front so the wardrobe reads as part of the architecture rather than a freestanding box.

Inside, use PAX interior organizers for the layout that fits your clothes: double hanging rails on one side, shelves and drawers on the other. Add doors in a shaker style if your budget allows, or keep the standard doors and change only the handles. This is a semi-permanent project, so it is best for a place you plan to stay in for a while.

sections.title: 7. Build a Desk From an ALEX Drawer Unit and a Tabletop
sections.content:
One ALEX drawer unit plus a simple tabletop gives you a desk with real storage and a clean, custom look. Rest the tabletop on the drawer unit at one end and a matching leg at the other, and you have a workspace sized exactly to your wall, with drawers for supplies instead of a tangle of cables and clutter.

Choose a tabletop depth of around 24 inches so a laptop, a notebook and a lamp all fit comfortably. Add a cable tray underneath and a small desk organizer on top to keep the surface clear. This setup costs less than most desks, comes apart easily for a move, and works in a living room corner as well as a bedroom.

sections.title: 8. Turn a KALLAX Into a Rolling Kitchen Island
sections.content:
A two-by-two KALLAX on casters, topped with a butcher block board, becomes a kitchen island with open storage on both sides. The cubes hold cookbooks, mixing bowls and small appliances, while the top gives you extra prep space that a small kitchen almost never has.

Use locking casters so the island stays put while you chop, and overhang the top by about an inch on each side for a finished edge. Add a towel bar to one side and a few hooks for measuring cups to make it work even harder. This is a renter-friendly hack that rolls out of the way when you need floor space for guests.

sections.title: 9. Make a MALM Bed Look Custom With an Upholstered Headboard Wall
sections.content:
A MALM bed frame is a clean, low platform, and it pairs beautifully with a wall of upholstered panels behind it. Mount fabric-covered foam panels in a row above the bed, floor to head height or a little above, and the bed suddenly looks like a designer piece with a statement headboard.

Pick a fabric that matches your bedding in a slightly darker tone so the panels read as one feature. Use removable adhesive strips or a French cleat if you rent, so the panels come down without wall damage. Add two small wall lights on either side and the whole sleeping corner feels finished, even in a room with no other built-ins.

sections.title: 10. Turn an IVAR Cabinet Into a Pantry With Doors
sections.content:
An IVAR cabinet with its plain pine frame becomes a pantry when you add doors, paint it, and fit it with interior shelves sized for food storage. The untreated wood takes paint beautifully, so you can match it to your kitchen cabinets or make it a contrasting accent piece in a hallway.

Inside, use clear bins and labels so cans, grains and snacks stay visible and nothing gets lost at the back. Add small casters if you want the pantry to roll into a gap beside the fridge. Because IVAR is solid pine, it also accepts new hardware easily, so swap the standard knobs for cup pulls to complete the custom look.

sections.title: 11. Use MOSSLANDA Picture Ledges as a Book Wall
sections.content:
MOSSLANDA picture ledges are made for frames, but they make a wonderful low-profile book display. Mount three or four ledges in a vertical column or a staggered row, and stand books with their covers facing out, like a bookshop display, instead of packed spine-out on a deep shelf.

This works especially well in narrow hallways and above a desk, where a full bookcase would block the walkway. Rotate the displayed books every few weeks to keep the wall feeling fresh, and keep the heaviest books on the lowest ledge. Use proper wall anchors, since books are heavier than picture frames, and mount into studs wherever possible.

sections.title: 12. Turn a RASKOG Cart Into a Bar Cart
sections.content:
A RASKOG utility cart becomes a bar cart with almost no work: line the trays with a washable liner, add a few glasses, a small plant and a tray for bottles, and it is ready to roll out for guests and tuck away after. The three tiers keep everything visible, which is exactly what a bar cart needs.

Spray-paint the frame a metallic or matte black if you want it to look less utilitarian, and add small caster stops so it stays put on hard floors. The same cart also works as a coffee station, a craft cart or a bathroom caddy, so it is one of the most flexible hacks on this list. It needs no tools and no wall fixings at all.

sections.title: 13. Give a LACK Table a Stone-Look Top
sections.content:
A LACK side table is the cheapest piece in the catalogue, and it is also one of the easiest to transform. Cover the top with a stone-look adhesive film or a thin marble-patterned tile, trim the edges neatly, and the little table suddenly looks like a boutique accent piece beside a sofa or bed.

Take your time with the corners, wrapping the film smoothly and trimming with a sharp blade for a clean edge. Pair the finished table with a small lamp or a stack of books and nobody will guess its origin. This is a ten-minute, fully reversible project, and if the film ever wears out you can simply peel it off and start again.

sections.title: 14. Turn a BEKVAM Step Stool Into a Plant Stand
sections.content:
A BEKVAM step stool is sturdy, compact and made of beech, which makes it a perfect plant stand. Paint it a color that matches your pots, or leave the wood natural and seal it, then place plants at two heights: one on the top step and one on the lower step, with a trailing plant to soften the edges.

The stool still works as a step stool when you need to reach a high shelf, so it earns its floor space twice over. In a bathroom, use it for rolled towels and a candle instead of plants. Because it is small and freestanding, this hack suits renters and anyone who likes to rearrange often.

sections.title: 15. Build a Fold-Down Desk From a NORBERG Wall-Mounted Table
sections.content:
A NORBERG wall-mounted drop-leaf table folds down into a desk and folds flat against the wall when you are done, which makes it ideal for apartments where a permanent desk would eat the room. Mount it at desk height near an outlet, add a small wall shelf above it for supplies, and you have a complete workstation in about two feet of wall.

Use a comfortable chair that can slide underneath or be stored elsewhere, and keep a small basket on the shelf for notebooks and chargers so setup takes seconds. This hack does require wall fixings rated for the load, so mount into a stud and check with your landlord if you rent. Folded up, it looks like a simple wall panel.

sections.title: 16. Turn an IVAR Shelf Unit Into an Entryway Bench
sections.content:
An IVAR side unit with a cushion on top and hooks on the wall above it becomes a complete entryway station. The open shelves below hold shoes in baskets, the cushion gives you a seat for putting them on, and the hooks take coats, bags and keys in one spot by the door.

Paint the unit to match your hallway trim, or stain it a warm walnut for a more furniture-like feel. Add a small tray on top for sunglasses and mail, and a boot mat underneath to protect the floor. This is a freestanding hack, so it works in rentals, and the whole station can be assembled in an afternoon with basic tools.

sections.title: 17. Add Doors, Legs and Hardware to Open KALLAX Cubes
sections.content:
Open KALLAX cubes can look unfinished, but door inserts, drawer inserts and new hardware change that completely. Add doors to the cubes that hold clutter, leave a few open for display, and fit the whole unit with matching knobs or leather pulls so it reads as a designed cabinet rather than a storage grid.

Raising the unit on short legs finishes the transformation, lifting it off the floor and giving it the stance of real furniture. Mix textures inside the open cubes, with baskets on one row and books on another, so the closed and open sections balance each other. Everything here is reversible, which makes it a safe first hack for a new apartment.

sections.title: How to Plan an IKEA Hack for a Small Apartment
sections.content:
Start by measuring twice: the space, the piece and the route it takes to get into the room. Many hacks fail because a finished unit is an inch too tall for a ceiling gap or too wide for a doorway, so write down the width, depth and height of both the space and the piece before you buy anything.

Next, decide how permanent the hack should be. If you rent, favor changes that come apart: legs, adhesive trim, freestanding units and paint on untreated wood like IVAR. Save wall-mounted and built-in projects for a home you own, or get written permission first.

Keep the tool list short. Most of the hacks here need a drill, a level, a tape measure and a screwdriver. Borrow or rent anything bigger rather than buying it for one project. Finally, anchor tall furniture to the wall, even if the hack does not call for it, since a loaded bookcase or wardrobe can tip.

sections.title: Final Thoughts
sections.content:
The best IKEA hacks are not the most complicated ones. They are the ones that solve a real problem in your apartment: a desk that disappears, a closet that reaches the ceiling, a dresser that finally looks like it belongs. Start with one piece, one weekend and one change, and see how much better the room feels.

Once you have a first hack under your belt, the rest get easier. You will know which pieces you like living with, which finishes suit your home, and which projects are worth the effort. Small apartments reward this kind of thinking more than big ones do, because every piece has to work harder and every inch counts.

faqs.answer: Many are. Freestanding hacks like adding legs to a MALM dresser, rolling a KALLAX island or styling a RASKOG cart need no wall fixings at all. Wall-mounted projects like a BESTA media wall or a NORBERG desk need drilling, so check your lease or ask your landlord first, and use proper anchors.
faqs.question: Are IKEA hacks renter-friendly?

faqs.answer: Most hacks need only a drill, a level, a tape measure and a screwdriver. Paint, adhesive film and trim are beginner-friendly, and pre-cut boards from a hardware store remove the need for a saw. Start with a simple project like a LACK table top before attempting a built-in wardrobe.
faqs.question: Do I need advanced tools to hack IKEA furniture?

faqs.answer: KALLAX is the classic starting point because it is cheap, sturdy and endlessly adaptable, from window seats to room dividers to kitchen islands. MALM and BILLY are close behind, since a set of legs or a strip of trim transforms them with very little effort.
faqs.question: Which IKEA piece is best for a first hack?

faqs.answer: Close the gaps, unify the finish and upgrade the details. Trim that meets the wall and ceiling, one consistent paint color, real furniture legs and quality hardware do more than any single expensive change. Styling matters too: fewer, larger objects on display look more custom than a crowded shelf.
faqs.question: How do I make IKEA furniture look less like flat-pack?
